title: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
summary: Exact unlearning with SISA, certified removal, why gradient ascent collapses and how NPO fixes it, WHP and RMU, how TOFU and MUSE measure forgetting, the attacks that undo it, robust methods, and a lab.
outcomes: Explain what exact unlearning guarantees and compute how SISA's sharding and slicing cut retraining cost
Define (epsilon, delta)-certified removal and compute a Newton-step removal for logistic regression
Explain why gradient ascent collapses and how NPO's adaptive weight slows divergence
Describe how Who's Harry Potter and RMU replace knowledge instead of pushing it down
Compute a truth ratio, a KS forget quality and a PrivLeak score against a retrained model
Explain why fine-tuning, direction removal and 4-bit quantization recover approximately unlearned knowledge
Compare tamper-resistant training, distillation and pretraining data filtering as routes to robust unlearning
Run an unlearning method, track forget quality and utility, and test a quantized and a relearned copy

lessons.title: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA

blocks.md:
A trained model is a compressed summary of its training data, and large models can memorize parts of it verbatim. So deleting a row from the database does not delete its influence: the weights still carry it. Three pressures make this matter: privacy law (the right to erasure in the EU's General Data Protection Regulation, GDPR, which lets a person demand that their personal data be deleted, and which motivated Bourtoule et al.), copyrighted text that should not have been trained on, and hazardous knowledge (for example, bioweapon details) that a lab wants out of a released model.

**Machine unlearning** is the task of removing the influence of a chosen **forget set** of training data (or of a body of knowledge) from an already trained model, while keeping everything else the model can do.

The gold standard is simple to state. Let $D$ be the training set and $D_f \subset D$ the forget set. **Exact unlearning** produces a model that could have come from training on the remaining data, $D$ minus $D_f$, from the start. Retraining from scratch on the remaining data achieves this by definition, and it is the reference every other method is measured against.

The problem is cost. Llama-2-7B took over 184K GPU-hours to pretrain (as reported by Eldan and Russinovich), and deletion requests arrive one at a time. Nobody retrains a 7B model per request.

**SISA training** (Bourtoule et al., 2019) keeps the guarantee of exact unlearning but makes retraining cheaper by limiting how far any one point can spread. It changes how you train *before* any deletion happens:

1. **Sharded**: split $D$, which holds $N$ points, into $S$ disjoint shards of about $N/S$ points each.
2. **Isolated**: train a separate model on each shard.
3. **Sliced**: inside a shard, add data in $R$ slices and checkpoint before each one.
4. **Aggregated**: combine the shard models at inference, for example by majority vote.

blocks.title: SISA: sharded, isolated, sliced, aggregated

scenes.caption: Sharded: split the training set into S disjoint shards (here S = 4). Every point lives in exactly one shard.
Isolated: train one constituent model per shard, with no information shared between them. A point can only influence the model of its own shard.
Aggregated: at inference every constituent model predicts and the simplest aggregation is a majority vote over labels.
A user asks to delete a point that sits in shard B. Models A, C and D never saw it, so they are already exactly what retraining without it would give.
Only model B is retrained on shard B minus the point. The cost is one shard, about N/S points, instead of all N.

blocks.title: Slicing: resume from the last checkpoint that never saw the point

scenes.caption: A toy SISA layout: N = 16 points, S = 4 shards, R = 4 slices per shard (one point per slice here). Columns are slices in the order they are added to training.
Shard B's model is trained incrementally: slice 1, then slices 1 and 2, and so on. The parameters are saved to disk just before each new slice is added.
Point d6 must be unlearned. It sits in slice 3 of shard B. Every training step from slice 3 onward saw it; the checkpoint saved before slice 3 never did.
Load the checkpoint saved before slice 3 and redo only the later training on the remaining points. Shards A, C, D and the first two slices of B are untouched. The price is storing the checkpoints.

blocks.md: For a single request, sharding means retraining one shard instead of the whole set. Slicing adds more: if the deleted point sits in slice $r$, you resume from the checkpoint saved before slice $r$ and redo only the later training. Under the paper's simplifying assumptions (uniform requests, training time proportional to the number of samples processed, epochs rebalanced so sliced and unsliced training cost the same), the best case, a point in the last slice, gives this speed-up for one request:

blocks.caption: With the paper's main setting S = 20, R = 50 this is 20x from sharding and 510x combined in the best case. Averaged over where the point falls, slicing gains at most 1.5x (the paper's Eq. 4), so about 30x combined; batched requests lower it further.

blocks.md: Where do these numbers come from? Sharding: a full retrain processes all $N$ points, a shard retrain only $N/S$, so the cost falls by a factor of $S$. Slicing: a shard model is trained in $R$ stages, where stage $i$ trains on the first $i$ slices, each slice being one $R$-th of the shard. Over all stages that is $1 + 2 + \dots + R$ slices of data, which sums to $R$ times $(R+1)$ over 2, so to match plain training for $e$ epochs, each stage runs $2e$ divided by $(R+1)$ epochs. A point in the last slice means redoing only the last stage: $N/S$ points for $2e$ divided by $(R+1)$ epochs, against $e$ times $N$ for a full retrain. Divide and the ratio is $(R+1)$ times $S$ over 2: with $R = 50$ and $S = 20$ that is $51 \times 20 / 2 = 510$.

Requests accumulate. If $K$ requests are batched and each hits a uniformly random shard, the expected fraction of shards that must be retrained is $1 - (1 - 1/S)^K$ (this is the batch-cost formula from the paper divided by $N$, ignoring the $K$ deleted points themselves). The reasoning: one request misses a given shard with probability $1 - 1/S$, so $K$ independent requests all miss it with probability $(1 - 1/S)$ to the power $K$, and the shard is hit, and must be retrained, with the remaining probability. Averaged over shards, that probability is also the expected fraction hit. With $S = 20$ and $K = 20$: $1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 0.642$.

blocks.title: How much of the model a batch of K deletions touches

scenes.caption: With S = 20 shards and uniformly random requests, one request touches 1/20 of the model. 20 requests already touch 64.2% of the shards in expectation.

At K = 3S = 60 requests, 95.4% of shards need retraining, close to retraining everything. This matches the paper's observation that sharding helps while requests stay below about three times the shard count.
Few shards (S = 5) saturate almost immediately. More shards delay saturation but make each constituent model a weaker learner because it sees less data.

blocks.md: Measured results are therefore modest. With 20 shards and 50 slices, SISA was 4.63x faster than retraining from scratch on Purchase (customers' shopping records over 600 products, 8 requests) and 2.45x on SVHN (Street View House Numbers, photos of house-number digits, 18 requests), at under 2 percentage points of accuracy loss. On ImageNet the speed-up was only 1.36x, with a large accuracy drop that transfer learning (starting each shard model from a network already trained on other data) reduced. The reason is the **weak learner** problem: each shard model sees only $1/S$ of the data, which hurts most on complex tasks.

SISA is a training-time design decision. It cannot be retrofitted onto a model that was already trained on all the data, which is the situation for every existing LLM. That is why the rest of this course is about **approximate** unlearning: editing an existing model so it behaves *as if* it had been retrained. The next lesson makes "as if" precise and shows the one setting where it can be certified; for LLMs there is no guarantee.

Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

blocks.question: A SISA system with S = 20 shards batches 60 uniformly random deletion requests before retraining. Roughly what fraction of the shard models must be retrained?
options: About 95%, almost every shard is hit at least once
About 5%, one shard per batch
About 33%, since 60 / 20 = 3 requests per shard on average
100% exactly, because 60 is larger than 20
blocks.explain: Each shard escapes all 60 requests with probability (1 - 1/20)^60, about 0.046, so about 95.4% of shards are hit at least once. It is not exactly 100% because some shards can get zero requests by chance. This saturation is why SISA's measured speed-ups shrink as requests pile up.

blocks.question: What does slicing cost in exchange for faster unlearning?
options: Lower accuracy, because each slice model is a weaker learner
Storage, because parameters must be checkpointed before every slice
Privacy, because checkpoints leak the deleted point
Nothing, slicing is free
blocks.explain: Slicing changes when data is added inside a shard, not how much data a model sees, so the paper reports no accuracy cost. The overhead is storing the parameter state before each slice is introduced so that retraining can resume from the last checkpoint that never saw the point. Old checkpoints that contain the point must be discarded after unlearning.

lessons.title: Certified removal: what 'as if retrained' means formally

blocks.md:
SISA keeps the exact guarantee by changing how the model is trained. For a model that is already trained, the cheaper hope is to edit its weights so the result is *close* to what retraining would give. But close in what sense?

A tiny example from Guo et al. (2020) shows why close weights are not enough. Train a linear regressor with weight decay on the points $(e_1, 1), (e_2, 2), \dots, (e_d, d)$, where $e_i$ is the $i$-th standard basis vector (all zeros except a 1 in position $i$). The weight $w_i$ is non-zero exactly when the point $(e_i, i)$ was in the training set. A removal method that leaves $w_i$ small but non-zero is very close to the retrained weights, yet anyone who looks at $w_i$ can tell the point was there.

The fix is to compare *distributions* of models, not single weight vectors. Training is usually randomized (initialization, data order, added noise), so a learning algorithm $A$ applied to data $D$ produces a random model. Ginart et al. (2019) called a deletion operation exact when its output and $A$ trained on $D$ without the point are equal in distribution, which is what SISA achieves, and noted that the definition relaxes to a bound on how far apart the two distributions may be.

Guo et al. made that relaxation precise as **certified removal**. Let $M$ be the removal mechanism: it takes the trained model $A(D)$, the data $D$ and the point $x$ to remove, and returns an edited model.

blocks.tex: e^{-\varepsilon} \le \frac{P\big(M(A(D), D, x) \in T\big)}{P\big(A(D \setminus x) \in T\big)} \le e^{\varepsilon} \quad \text{for every set of models } T
blocks.caption: In words: for every set T of possible models, the chance that removal lands in T is within a factor e to the epsilon of the chance that retraining without x lands there. epsilon = 0 is exact removal.

blocks.md:
Read $\varepsilon$ as a budget: at $\varepsilon = 0.1$ the two probabilities differ by at most a factor of about 1.105. The relaxed **$(\varepsilon, \delta)$-certified removal** lets the bound fail with probability at most $\delta$. Guo et al. point out that the guarantee means membership inference attacks (guessing from a model whether a point was in its training data; lesson 5 uses them) cannot succeed on removed data.

This is the shape of **differential privacy** (DP: a training algorithm whose output distribution changes by at most a factor $e^{\varepsilon}$ when one training point is added or removed; optional background in the Privacy engineering course, lesson 8), with one change: the two things compared are the trained-then-edited model and the never-trained one. A differentially private training algorithm is already certified for removal with $M$ doing nothing. But privacy is not required: a nearest-neighbour classifier is not differentially private, yet deleting one of its points is exact and takes constant time.

Guo et al. give a mechanism for linear models with L2 regularization and a convex, differentiable loss, such as logistic regression. Training minimizes $L(w; D) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell(w^\top x_i, y_i) + \frac{\lambda n}{2}\lVert w\rVert_2^2$, whose minimizer $w^*$ is unique.

To remove the last point $(x_n, y_n)$, start from two facts. At the optimum $\nabla L(w^*; D) = 0$. And the loss on the remaining data $D'$ is the full loss minus that point's term and minus $\frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert w\rVert_2^2$. So at $w^*$ the remaining loss has gradient $-\Delta$, where $\Delta = \lambda w^* + \nabla \ell(w^{*\top} x_n, y_n)$ is the removed point's pull. Newton's method fits a quadratic to the loss using the **Hessian** $H$, the matrix of second derivatives (how the gradient itself changes as $w$ moves), and jumps to that quadratic's minimum by subtracting $H^{-1}$ times the gradient. One Newton step on $D'$ from $w^*$ gives the removal update:

blocks.tex: w^- = w^* + H_{w^*}^{-1}\,\Delta, \qquad H_{w^*} = \nabla^2 L(w^*; D')
blocks.caption: H^-1 Delta is the influence function of the removed point: a first-order estimate of how far the optimum moves when that point is dropped. The Hessian can be formed before any request arrives (cost d^2 n); inverting it costs d^3 at removal time, for d features.

blocks.md: For least squares the loss is exactly quadratic, so one Newton step lands on the retrained optimum and removal is exact. For logistic regression it does not quite, and what is left is the **gradient residual** $\lVert\nabla L(w^-; D')\rVert_2$, which is zero only at the true optimum. Guo et al. bound it by $4\gamma C^2 / (\lambda^2 (n-1))$ (their Theorem 1, where $C$ bounds the norm of any one point's loss gradient and $\gamma$ bounds how fast the loss's curvature $\ell''$ can change, its Lipschitz constant; for logistic loss with $\lVert x_i \rVert \le 1$, $\gamma = 1/4$ and $C = 1$), so it shrinks as the dataset grows. Their Corollary 1 gives a much tighter bound computed from the data itself.

blocks.title: Newton-step removal on 8 points (computed)

scenes.caption: Logistic regression without a bias term on 8 points of norm at most 1, lambda = 0.1. The trained weights w* = (1.337, 0.825) put the decision boundary on the line x2 = -1.621 x1.
Remove the + point at (0.8, -0.2). One Newton step gives w- = (1.2421, 0.9461), and the boundary rotates to slope -1.3128.
Retraining from scratch on the 7 remaining points gives (1.2424, 0.9466), slope -1.3125. The lines coincide at this scale: the weights moved 0.154 and missed the retrained optimum by 0.0006.

blocks.md: The numbers, from a script that fits both models by Newton's method to convergence: the removed point's pull is $\Delta = (-0.097, 0.140)$, so at $w^*$ the remaining loss has a gradient of norm 0.170. After the Newton step the gradient residual is 0.00073, about 230 times smaller. Corollary 1's data-dependent bound is 0.0149. Theorem 1's worst-case bound is 14.3, useless at $n = 8$, which is why the paper derives the data-dependent one.

A small residual still leaks: its *direction* can point at the removed data. Guo et al. hide it with **loss perturbation** (from Chaudhuri et al.): train on $L(w; D) + b^\top w$ for a random vector $b$ drawn once. A model with residual $u$ is then the exact optimum for the slightly different vector $b - u$, so if $b$'s density changes by at most a factor $e^{\varepsilon}$ when $b$ moves by the residual bound $\varepsilon'$, removal is $\varepsilon$-certified. Gaussian $b$ with scale $\sigma = c\,\varepsilon'/\varepsilon$, where $c = \sqrt{2\ln(1.5/\delta)}$, gives $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-certified removal.

Residual bounds add up over removals, so the paper's Algorithm 2 keeps a running total and retrains from scratch once it exceeds $\sigma\varepsilon/c$. With $\varepsilon = 1$ and $\delta = 10^{-4}$, $c = 4.385$; covering our one removal (bound 0.0149) needs $\sigma \ge 0.065$. The worked example used $b = 0$ to keep the geometry visible.

It is cheap where it applies. On MNIST a certified linear model took 0.04 seconds per removal against 15.6 seconds to train (Guo et al., Table 1). Deep networks are covered only partly: the certified linear model sits on top of a feature extractor that is either trained on public data, so nothing private needs removing from it, or trained with differential privacy.

For an LLM every ingredient breaks. The loss is not convex, so there is no unique optimum and no bound on a Newton step's error. The Hessian has one row and one column per parameter, about $4.9 \times 10^{19}$ entries for a 7B model. So for LLMs "as if retrained" stays an informal target: the methods of lessons 3 and 4 carry no certificate, and they are judged empirically, against an actually retrained model (lesson 5) and by attacking them (lesson 6).

Weights that are close to the retrained weights are not removal. Certified removal is a statement about the *distribution* of models, and it needs randomness added at training time to hide what the leftover error reveals.

Certified removal asks that the edited model be distributed almost like a model retrained without the point, within a factor $e^{\varepsilon}$. For L2-regularized linear models a Newton step plus training-time noise achieves it cheaply. For LLMs no such certificate exists.

blocks.question: You use Newton-step removal on an L2-regularized least-squares regressor. How much loss perturbation noise do you need for certified removal?
options: The same as for logistic regression, since both are linear models
A lot, because least squares is not differentially private
None: the loss is quadratic, so one Newton step lands exactly on the retrained optimum (epsilon = 0)
It cannot be certified, because the Hessian changes with w
blocks.explain: The Newton step uses a local quadratic model of the loss, which is exact for least squares: its Hessian does not depend on w. The gradient residual is exactly zero, so Guo et al. note no perturbation is needed. Logistic loss is not quadratic, which is why it leaves a residual to mask.

blocks.question: A removal method leaves your model's weights within 0.001 of the retrained weights for every request. Why is that not, by itself, a guarantee?
options: Because 0.001 is too large for any real model
Because the leftover difference can be systematic and reveal the removed point; a guarantee must bound the distribution of models, which needs randomness such as loss perturbation
Because retraining is random too, so weight distances mean nothing
It is a guarantee: close weights give the same predictions
blocks.explain: In Guo et al.'s basis-vector example, a small but non-zero weight is close to the retrained value of zero yet reveals that the point was trained on. Certified removal bounds how much the whole distribution of possible models can differ, which is why the residual is masked with noise drawn at training time.

lessons.title: Approximate unlearning: gradient ascent, collapse and NPO

blocks.md: **Gradient ascent (GA)** maximizes the usual next-token loss on the forget set, which is the same as minimizing the log-likelihood the model assigns to forget text. Recall from pretraining that the loss is $-\log p_\theta(y \mid x)$ summed over tokens, where $\theta$ stands for the model's weights; GA simply flips its sign:

Why does this go wrong? Look at a single token with softmax output $p$ over the vocabulary and correct token $y$. The gradient of $\log p_y$ with respect to the logit $z_y$ is $1 - p_y$: since $\log p_y = z_y - \log\sum_j e^{z_j}$, differentiating gives $1 - p_y$, the pretraining cross-entropy gradient with its sign flipped. As unlearning succeeds, $p_y$ goes to 0 and the push goes to 1, its maximum. Nothing in the loss says "this one is forgotten, stop", because $\log p_y$ has no lower bound: it heads to minus infinity.

blocks.caption: The push on an already-forgotten example never fades, so weights drift without limit (Zhang et al. show the drift can be linear in the number of steps).

blocks.prompt: Predict: you run gradient ascent with a retain loss for 400 steps on a tiny classifier. The forget answer is gone by step 25. What happens to the weights between step 25 and step 400?
blocks.reveal: They keep moving, roughly linearly. In the toy run below the distance from the starting weights goes from 8.3 at step 25 to 356.9 at step 400, and the displaced probability eventually damages a retain example even though a retain loss is present. In a real LLM every weight is shared by all knowledge, so this drift is what **catastrophic collapse** looks like: utility falls to zero and outputs become gibberish.

blocks.title: Toy run: gradient ascent vs NPO, both with a retain loss

scenes.caption: Simplified model: a 4-class softmax classifier on 3 features, trained on one forget example and two retain examples that share features with it. All start at p = 0.959. Each run then takes 400 steps of its unlearning loss plus a retain loss.
Gradient ascent (GA) on the forget example, plus the normal loss on the retain examples. By step 25 the forget answer is gone (p = 0.000) and the retain examples are fine.

But GA never stops. The weight drift (L2 distance from the starting weights) keeps growing roughly linearly, to 356.9 by step 400. Around step 120 the displaced mass lands on a retain class and one retain example drops to 0.75 despite the retain loss.

NPO with the same retain loss: the forget answer falls to 0.058 by step 25 and 0.001 by step 400, while its weight drift levels off (3.5 at step 25, 6.4 at step 400). Its retain examples end at 0.998.

blocks.md: This matches LLM experiments. TOFU is a benchmark of invented authors that a model is fine-tuned on and then asked to forget; its **forget quality** score is high when the unlearned model looks statistically like the retrained one, and its **model utility** score measures what the model can still do (Lesson 5 builds both). On TOFU, Zhang et al. report that standalone gradient ascent makes model utility drop quickly to zero, with forget quality improving only briefly before falling too, and the model ends up generating gibberish (their example answer from GA with a retain loss is "narr narr narr narr"). On the news part of MUSE, a benchmark built from news articles and the Harry Potter books (also Lesson 5), plain GA scores 0 on both memorization metrics *and* 0 on utility. In practice GA only works with careful early stopping.

Two regularized variants are standard baselines in TOFU:

- **Gradient difference**: ascend on the forget set while descending on the retain set, $\mathcal{L} = -\mathcal{L}(D_f) + \mathcal{L}(D_r)$.
- **KL minimization**: ascend on the forget set while keeping the output distribution on retain data close to the original model's, measured by KL (Kullback-Leibler) divergence, which the prerequisite course defined as the average log ratio of the two models' probabilities: 0 only when they agree.

Both slow the damage but do not remove the cause: the forget term itself is still unbounded.

**Negative Preference Optimization (NPO)** (Zhang, Lin, Bai and Mei, 2024) fixes the cause. Recall that DPO trains on pairs of a preferred and a dispreferred answer, measured against a frozen reference model. NPO keeps only the dispreferred half: every forget example is a negative, and the reference $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is the model before unlearning.

blocks.caption: In words: 2 over beta times the average over forget examples of log of 1 plus (current probability over reference probability) to the power beta. Bounded below by 0. Its gradient equals the GA gradient multiplied by a per-example weight that shrinks once the example is already unlearned.

Minimizing $\log(1 + r^ eta)$ pushes $r$ down, like gradient ascent, but the loss can never fall below $\log 1 = 0$, so there is no minus infinity to chase. Differentiate: the gradient of $r^ eta$ is $ eta r^ eta$ times $
abla\log\pi_	heta$, so the gradient of the loss is $ rac{2}{ eta}$ times $ rac{ eta r^ eta}{1 + r^ eta}$ times $
abla\log\pi_	heta$. The betas cancel, leaving the GA gradient, $
abla\log\pi_	heta$, times the weight $W$ below. At the start $r = 1$ and $W = 1$; as $r$ falls, $W$ falls with it.

blocks.caption: In words: the weight W is 2 r to the beta, over r to the beta plus 1. The figure's horizontal axis is log base 10 of r, so -1 means the probability has fallen to a tenth of the reference.

blocks.title: Per-example gradient weight: GA vs NPO

scenes.caption: At the start of unlearning the model equals the reference, r = 1 (x = 0), and both methods push with weight 1.
With beta = 1, once an example's probability has fallen to a tenth of the reference (x = -1) NPO's weight is 0.182; at a hundredth it is 0.020. Already-forgotten examples stop pulling the weights.
As beta shrinks toward 0 the NPO curve flattens toward 1, recovering gradient ascent exactly, as the paper proves. Beta is the knob between aggressive and self-limiting.

blocks.md: The paper proves, in a simplified setting, that GA diverges linearly while NPO diverges only logarithmically, which is exponentially slower. Empirically, NPO with a retain loss (NPO+RT) was the only method in their tests to reach forget quality above 0.05 (forget quality is a p-value, and 0.05 is the usual cutoff below which two samples are judged different) on 20% and 30% forget splits that the NPO authors built by extending TOFU (TOFU itself ships 1%, 5% and 10%), and with tuned loss weights it exceeded 0.05 forget quality with model utility above 0.55 even when forgetting 50% and 90% of TOFU.

Where do the two rates come from? A single-logit simplification shows it. Let one forget example's answer have logit $s$ and probability $p = \sigma(s) = 1/(1 + e^{-s})$, and let the step size be $\eta$. Gradient ascent moves $s$ down by $\eta(1 - p)$ per step, which is about $\eta$ once $p$ is small: a constant push, so linear drift.

NPO multiplies that push by $W$, and once $r$ is small, $W \approx 2r^{\beta}$. With $\beta = 1$ the push is about $2\eta p / p_{\text{ref}}$, and $p \approx e^{s}$ when $s$ is very negative, so the push shrinks exponentially as $s$ falls. Solving $ds/dt = -k\,e^{s}$ gives $e^{-s}$ growing linearly in $t$, so $s$ falls like $-\ln t$: every tenfold increase in steps moves it by about the same amount.

A script with $s$ starting at 3 ($p_{\text{ref}} = 0.953$), $\beta = 1$ and $\eta = 0.5$: gradient ascent's logit has moved by 29 at step 100, 479 at step 1,000 and 4,979 at step 10,000. NPO's has moved by 6.8, 9.9 and 12.3, and its weight $W$ is down to 0.002 by step 1,000. The toy classifier above shows the same pattern in its weights: from step 25 to step 400, GA's drift grows from 8.3 to 356.9, NPO's only from 3.5 to 6.4.

A common follow-up, **SimNPO** (Fan et al., 2024), drops the reference model. It replaces NPO's $\beta \log(\pi_\theta / \pi_{\text{ref}})$ with SimPO's length-normalized $(\beta / |y|) \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)$ (SimPO is a reference-free variant of DPO; optional background in the DPO variants course, lesson 6). The motivation is what the authors call reference model bias: at the start $\pi_\theta = \pi_{\text{ref}}$, so NPO's weight is about 1 for every example and early NPO behaves like gradient ascent.

"Loss on the forget set went up" (or its perplexity, $e$ to the average per-token loss, as in the prerequisite course) is not evidence of good unlearning. GA can drive that loss arbitrarily high by wrecking the model. Always read forget metrics next to utility metrics and next to the retrained reference.

Gradient ascent fails because its objective is unbounded: forgotten examples keep pushing. NPO is gradient ascent with an adaptive weight that fades once an example's probability falls below the reference, so unlearning slows down instead of collapsing.

blocks.question: During NPO with beta = 1, a forget example's probability is now 1% of the reference model's. Compared with plain gradient ascent, how strongly does this example still push the weights?
options: Equally strongly, NPO only changes the loss value, not the gradient
About 2% as strongly, the weight is 2(0.01)/(0.01 + 1) = 0.020
About 50% as strongly, the weight bottoms out at 0.5
Twice as strongly, because NPO doubles the gradient
blocks.explain: NPO's gradient is the GA gradient times W = 2r^b / (r^b + 1). With r = 0.01 and b = 1 that is 0.02 / 1.01, about 0.020. The weight stays near 1 only for very small beta, where NPO behaves like GA; there is no floor at 0.5, it keeps falling toward 0.

blocks.question: A teammate runs gradient ascent on a forget set and reports success because forget-set perplexity rose from 8 to 4,000. What is the most important missing check?
options: Whether the learning rate was warmed up
Utility on retain and general data, compared with a retrained reference
Whether the forget-set perplexity is above 10,000
Whether the model still refuses harmful prompts
blocks.explain: Gradient ascent can raise forget-set loss without limit by damaging the whole model, which is catastrophic collapse. The meaningful question is whether the model now behaves like one never trained on the forget set while keeping its other abilities, so you need retain and general utility and a comparison with the retrained model.

lessons.title: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU

blocks.md: Gradient ascent asks the model to be *wrong* about the forget data. A better target is to be *ignorant*: produce what a model that never read the data would produce. Eldan and Russinovich point out two problems with pushing down the true tokens. In "Harry Potter went up to him and said, Hello. My name is" the next word is Harry, and penalizing it unlearns what "my name is" means. And if "Ron" is pushed down in "Harry Potter's two best friends are", the most likely token simply becomes "Hermione".

**Who's Harry Potter (WHP)** builds *generic predictions*: for every token in the books, an alternative next-token distribution approximating a model that never saw them. It combines two tricks.

1. **Reinforcement bootstrapping**: fine-tune a copy of the model further on the target text, giving a **reinforced model**. Tokens whose logits rise under reinforcement are the story-specific ones, so push them down.
2. **Anchored terms**: replace idiosyncratic names and terms with generic ones (they used GPT-4 to build a dictionary of about 1,500 such pairs), run the baseline model on the translated text, and use its predictions.

blocks.caption: v are logit vectors. The ReLU keeps only logits that the reinforcement increased. The paper uses alpha = 5.

blocks.md: The baseline model is then fine-tuned on the *original* text as input with the generic predictions as target labels. The unlearn set was the books (2.1M tokens) plus 1M tokens of synthetic discussions and wiki-like text, and about 1 GPU-hour of fine-tuning on Llama-2-7b-chat was enough, against the 184K GPU-hours of pretraining. General ability was checked on benchmarks such as ARC-Challenge (grade-school science multiple-choice questions that simple retrieval methods get wrong) and BoolQ (yes or no questions about a short Wikipedia passage).

After 20 fine-tuning steps on generic labels, familiarity has fallen from 0.290 to 0.040; benchmarks barely move.

blocks.md: The paper's own ablation is telling: reinforcement bootstrapping alone never reduced completion-based familiarity by more than a factor of 0.3. Anchored terms did most of the work, and they need a domain-specific dictionary of replacements (WHP generated it with GPT-4 entity extraction over passages of the books).

**RMU** (Representation Misdirection for Unlearning, Li et al., 2024) targets hazardous knowledge instead of a book series. It was released with **WMDP** (Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy), a public benchmark of 3,668 multiple-choice questions (1,273 biosecurity, 1,987 cybersecurity, 408 chemical security) that serve as a proxy for hazardous knowledge, filtered so the questions themselves are not hazardous. RMU changes internal activations (the hidden-state vectors a layer outputs for each token) rather than output tokens. The paper's main model is Zephyr-7B, a chat-tuned version of Mistral-7B, and general ability is measured with MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding): multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, virology among them.

scenes.caption: RMU edits a model through its hidden states, not its outputs. Only the MLP weights of three consecutive layers ending at layer l are trained (l = 7 for Zephyr-7B).

On forget text, the layer-l activation of every token is pulled toward c times a fixed random unit vector u. Large, meaningless activations early in the network leave later layers unable to use the knowledge.
On retain text, activations are pulled back toward the frozen original model's activations, weighted by alpha (1200 for Zephyr-7B). This keeps general skills.
Each update pairs a forget batch with a retain batch and minimizes forget loss plus alpha times retain loss. To unlearn bio and cyber together, RMU interleaves updates between the two topics.

After RMU: WMDP-Bio 31.2% and WMDP-Cyber 28.2%, close to chance, while overall MMLU only moves from 58.1% to 57.1%.
The collateral damage is in neighboring topics: MMLU virology falls from 52.4% to 25.9%, essentially chance. Hazardous and benign knowledge in the same field are hard to separate.

blocks.md: Near-chance accuracy on a multiple-choice proxy shows the model no longer *answers* those questions. It does not show the knowledge is gone from the weights. The WMDP authors say so themselves: because RMU edits only three layers it "perhaps obfuscates knowledge more than unlearns it", and in their appendix fine-tuning on the forget corpus recovered the performance.

Replacement methods give the model something specific to do instead: predict generic tokens (WHP) or produce scrambled activations on hazardous inputs (RMU). That avoids gradient ascent's collapse, but the target behavior is defined only on the inputs you trained on.

blocks.question: In WHP, the baseline model ranks Ron first and Hermione second, but the reinforced model, knowing the books better, ranks Hermione first. Only Hermione's logit rises under reinforcement. What does the generic-prediction formula do?
options: Pushes down both Ron and Hermione equally
Pushes down Hermione but leaves Ron as the top prediction
Leaves both unchanged because the ReLU blocks them
Removes both tokens from the vocabulary
blocks.explain: The formula only subtracts where the reinforced logit exceeds the baseline. Ron's logit did not rise, so it stays and remains the top prediction: the method reinforces a Harry Potter answer instead of removing it. The paper names this exact caveat, which is one reason it adds anchored-term translation.

blocks.question: RMU drops Zephyr-7B's WMDP-Bio accuracy from 63.7% to 31.2% while overall MMLU moves from 58.1% to 57.1%. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The hazardous knowledge has been erased from the weights
RMU has no side effects
The model no longer answers the proxy questions, with little general cost but real loss in nearby topics like virology
WMDP-Bio is now harder than random guessing
blocks.explain: Multiple-choice accuracy near 25% means the model no longer selects the right answers. The table also shows MMLU virology falling from 52.4% to 25.9%, so related benign knowledge was hit. Whether the knowledge is still in the weights is a separate question that fine-tuning attacks answer (Lesson 6).

lessons.title: Measuring forgetting: TOFU, MUSE and the forget-retain tradeoff

blocks.md: Evaluating approximate unlearning is hard for two reasons. First, "does not output it" is weaker than "does not know it". Second, the right target is not zero: a model that never saw the forget set still answers some forget questions from general knowledge, and a model that does *abnormally badly* on the forget set reveals that something was removed there. The yardstick is therefore the **retrained model**, and good unlearning means being indistinguishable from it.

**TOFU** (Task of Fictitious Unlearning, Maini et al., 2024) makes that reference cheap. It contains 200 fictitious author profiles with 20 question-answer pairs each, generated with GPT-4 so no pretrained model knows them. You fine-tune a model on all of them, then unlearn a forget split of 1%, 5% or 10% of the authors. Because the facts are invented, a **retain model** fine-tuned only on the other authors is a true never-saw-it reference.

The key per-question quantity is the **truth ratio**. Using length-normalized probabilities $P(a \mid q)^{1/|a|}$, compare a GPT-4 paraphrase $\tilde a$ of the correct answer with five perturbed, factually wrong answers $\hat a$ in the same template. The exponent $1/|a|$ is 1 over the answer's length in tokens, so it turns the answer's probability into a per-token geometric mean and long answers are not penalized just for having more tokens. Paraphrasing matters because the model was fine-tuned on one exact phrasing, which inflates its probability.

blocks.tex: R_{\text{truth}} = \frac{\frac{1}{|A_{\text{pert}}|}\sum_{\hat a \in A_{\text{pert}}} P(\hat a \mid q)^{1/|\hat a|}}{P(\tilde a \mid q)^{1/|\tilde a|}}
blocks.caption: In words: the average length-normalized probability of the wrong answers, divided by that of the paraphrased true answer. Small R means the model strongly prefers the true answer. R near 1 means it cannot tell true from false.

blocks.md: A worked example with assumed normalized probabilities: the paraphrased true answer gets 0.40 and the five wrong answers get 0.10, 0.08, 0.12, 0.06, 0.09 (mean 0.09). Then $R = 0.09 / 0.40 = 0.225$: the model knows the fact. If unlearning lowers the true answer to 0.09 with the wrong ones unchanged, $R = 1.0$: no preference left.

**Forget quality** is a statistical test, not an average. Compute truth ratios on every forget-set question for both the unlearned model and the retain model, then run a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test, named after the two mathematicians behind it, on the two distributions. The test sorts each sample into a cumulative curve (the fraction of values at or below each point) and measures the largest vertical gap between the two curves. Its p-value is the probability of a gap at least that large if both samples came from the same distribution. The p-value is the forget quality: high means you cannot tell the two models apart, low means the unlearned model is still distinguishable.

A worked example with 8 forget questions (TOFU uses every question in the split). The unlearned model's truth ratios are 0.21, 0.28, 0.33, 0.35, 0.41, 0.47, 0.52, 0.60; the retain model's on the same questions are 0.48, 0.55, 0.61, 0.66, 0.70, 0.74, 0.79, 0.88. Sort all 16 and record, at each value, the fraction of each sample at or below it: these step curves are the **empirical CDFs** (cumulative distribution functions). The largest gap between them is the KS statistic $D$, and scipy's `ks_2samp` turns it into an exact p-value.

The direction matters for the diagnosis. Ratios too *low* mean the model still prefers the true answers (under-unlearning); ratios far *above* the retain model's mean it now avoids them abnormally (over-unlearning). The test flags both, because it only asks whether the two distributions match.

blocks.title: Forget quality by hand: a KS test on 8 truth ratios

scenes.caption: All 16 truth ratios sorted together. Color a is the unlearned model, color b the retain model, on the same 8 forget questions.
Empirical CDF of the unlearned model: the fraction of its 8 ratios at or below each value. It reaches 0.75 by 0.47, because six of its ratios are that small.
Empirical CDF of the retain model. It stays at 0 until 0.48: a model that never saw these authors is much less sure of the true answers.
The gap between the two curves peaks at D = 0.75 (first at 0.47). The exact two-sample p-value for D = 0.75 with 8 and 8 values is 0.0186: forget quality 0.019, still distinguishable.
After more unlearning the unlearned model's ratios interleave with the retain model's. The largest gap is 0.125 and the p-value is 1.0: indistinguishable on this test.

blocks.md: **Model utility** is the harmonic mean of nine numbers: probability, ROUGE and truth ratio on the retain set, on real authors, and on world facts. ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) scores a generated answer by its word overlap with the reference answer. The harmonic mean of $n$ numbers is $n$ divided by the sum of their reciprocals, so a single value near 0 makes that sum huge and drags the result toward 0.

blocks.title: TOFU model utility: why a harmonic mean

scenes.caption: Model utility combines 3 metrics (probability, ROUGE, truth ratio) on 3 datasets (retain set, real authors, world facts). Made-up but typical values: arithmetic mean 0.809, harmonic mean 0.804.
Now one ability collapses to 0.02. The arithmetic mean only drops to 0.724, hiding the failure. The harmonic mean falls to 0.150, so the model is flagged as broken.

blocks.md: TOFU's baseline result was sobering. In the paper's runs with Phi-1.5 (a 1.3 billion parameter Microsoft model) with the 1% forget split (Llama-2-7B showed the same trends), gradient ascent, gradient difference, KL minimization and an "I don't know" preference baseline all failed to reach meaningful forget quality (every p-value below 0.001), and forgetting more than 1% caused severe utility drops. NPO, from Lesson 3, was later the first to reach forget quality above 0.05 on much larger splits.

**MUSE** (Machine Unlearning Six-Way Evaluation, Shi et al., 2024) widens the view to six criteria, three for data owners and three for deployers:

1. no verbatim memorization (VerbMem),
2. no knowledge memorization (KnowMem, QA about the forget set),
3. no privacy leakage (PrivLeak, from a membership inference attack),
4. utility preserved on the retain set,
5. scalability to large forget sets,
6. sustainability over sequential requests.

It uses two corpora: BBC news articles and the Harry Potter books, with 7B models. VerbMem prompts the model with the start of a forget-set text and scores its continuation by ROUGE overlap with the true continuation; KnowMem asks questions about the forget set and scores the answers the same way. A **membership inference attack** guesses, from how the model scores a text, whether that text was in training. The methods compared include GA, NPO, their retain-loss variants, and Task Vector, which fine-tunes a copy on the forget set and subtracts the resulting weight change from the original.

blocks.title: MUSE NEWS: forgetting vs utility (Llama-2 7B)

scenes.caption: KnowMem on the forget set (lower means less knowledge revealed). The retrained model still scores 33.1, not 0: some forget-set answers follow from general knowledge.

KnowMem on the retain set (utility, higher is better). GA reaches 0 forgetting by reaching 0 utility. Every method loses utility relative to the retrained model's 55.0 except Task Vector, which also forgot nothing.

blocks.md: **PrivLeak** compares how well a membership inference attack separates forget data from held-out data. The attack is Min-K% Prob, which averages the log probabilities of a text's k percent least likely tokens, since text seen in training has fewer very surprising tokens. Its success is the AUC (area under the ROC curve, the plot of the attack's true-positive rate against its false-positive rate over every threshold): the chance it ranks a random forget text as less familiar than a random held-out one, with 0.5 meaning no separation. PrivLeak is the unlearned model's AUC minus the retrained model's, divided by the retrained model's; it should be near 0. Large positive values mean **over-unlearning** (the forget set now looks *less* familiar than unseen data, which itself leaks membership) and large negative values mean **under-unlearning**.

On NEWS, gradient difference variants scored above +100% and KL-regularized variants about -96%; the paper reports that only one of eight methods avoided severe leakage, and that most degraded utility, scaled poorly to larger forget sets, and degraded over sequential requests.

MUSE's attack is a **population** attack: one scoring rule, Min-K% Prob, applied the same way to every text. Hayes et al. (2024) show that a **per-example** attack is much stronger. Their U-LiRA, an adaptation of the likelihood-ratio attack LiRA, trains many shadow models on random datasets that include the target example, unlearns the example from each with the method under test, and also retrains a twin without it. It fits a Gaussian to each group's logit-scaled confidence on that one example and asks which Gaussian the attacked model fits better.

On image classifiers and on fine-tuned PaLM 2, this showed that the population attacks common in the literature overestimate the privacy unlearning gives. Some forget examples stayed exposed while others were protected, and retain examples could leak more after unlearning. So a PrivLeak near 0 is necessary, not sufficient: the forget set as a whole looks unseen to one attack, which does not mean each person's data is hidden.

blocks.prompt: On MUSE NEWS, plain GA and plain NPO both score exactly 0 on VerbMem and KnowMem for the forget set, better than the retrained model's 20.8 and 33.1. Are they the best unlearning methods in the table?
blocks.reveal: No. Both also score 0 on retain-set KnowMem: the models are unusable. And scoring *below* the retrained model on the forget set is itself a signal, since a never-trained model would still answer about a third of those questions from general knowledge. The target is to match the retrained model, not to minimize forget metrics.

blocks.md: Unlearning is judged against the retrained model on two axes at once: forget metrics should match it (not undershoot it) and utility should stay near it. Under-unlearning and over-unlearning both leak that the data was there.

blocks.question: Your unlearned model gets a TOFU forget quality (KS-test p-value) of 0.0004. What does that mean?
options: The model forgot 99.96% of the forget set
The model's utility is 0.0004
The model is statistically indistinguishable from the retain model
The truth-ratio distribution on the forget set is very unlikely to come from the same distribution as the retain model's, so unlearning is incomplete or overshot
blocks.explain: Forget quality is the p-value of a two-sample KS test between the unlearned and retain models' truth-ratio distributions. A tiny p-value means the distributions clearly differ, which is poor unlearning in either direction. It is not a percentage of facts forgotten.

blocks.question: Why does TOFU aggregate its nine utility numbers with a harmonic mean rather than an arithmetic mean?
options: It is faster to compute
So that one collapsed ability drags the score down instead of being averaged away
Because the metrics have different units
So that utility is always at least 0.5
blocks.explain: A harmonic mean is dominated by its smallest inputs. In the example, one score dropping to 0.02 moves the arithmetic mean only to 0.724 but the harmonic mean to 0.150. The TOFU authors chose it for exactly this reason: they did not want low scores to be averaged out.

blocks.question: An unlearned model has Min-K% AUC 0.80 on forget versus held-out text, and the retrained model has 0.50. What is PrivLeak, and what does it say?
options: -37.5%: under-unlearning, the forget set still looks familiar
+30%: within the acceptable band
0%: both AUCs are above 0.5
+60%: over-unlearning, the forget set now looks less familiar than unseen text, which itself reveals it was targeted
blocks.explain: PrivLeak = (0.80 - 0.50) / 0.50 = +60%. In MUSE's orientation a large positive value means the forget texts look less familiar than held-out ones, which a never-trained model would not do. MUSE marks values outside -5% to 5% as leakage.

lessons.title: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks

blocks.md: Every method so far changes what the model *says*. The adversarial question is whether the knowledge is still recoverable from the weights. Lynch et al. (2024) ran eight such tests on the Who's Harry Potter model: prompts in other languages, jailbreak prompts, in-context relearning, relearning by fine-tuning, downstream question answering, latent knowledge probes, comparison with a trivial prompting baseline, and side effects on related domains. A jailbreak is a prompt crafted to get around the model's refusals, in-context relearning puts related text in the prompt, and a latent knowledge probe is a small classifier trained to read an answer straight out of the hidden states.

blocks.title: Relearning: a little data brings the knowledge back

scenes.caption: The provider runs unlearning and releases the weights. Standard evaluations look good.
Asked directly, the model gives a generic or wrong answer.
With open weights, the attacker fine-tunes on a small, possibly loosely related dataset. Lynch et al. used 800 or 8,000 sentences (about 1% or 10% of the books); Hu et al. used public, benign text.
The suppressed knowledge resurfaces, including facts that were not in the relearning data. Hu et al. recovered bioweapons-related knowledge by relearning on public medical articles.

blocks.md: Relearning attacks are cheap. Lynch et al. found fine-tuning on 8,000 sentences brought the WHP model close to the original's performance. The WMDP authors fine-tuned an RMU-unlearned Mistral-7B on the cybersecurity forget corpus and found RMU was unable to prevent recovery. Hu et al. (2024) showed that even *benign*, loosely related data works: general wiki text about the series brought back verbatim memorized passages. They conclude that current approximate methods suppress outputs rather than remove knowledge.

blocks.title: Recovering 'unlearned' WMDP-Bio accuracy (%)

scenes.caption: RMU on Zephyr-7B (original model 64.4%). Reading answers from intermediate layers (logit lens) fails, 31.8%, matching RMU's own probing results. Fine-tuning, direction removal, prefixes and pruning all bring most of it back.

NPO with a retain loss, trained by the authors on the same model: more resistant to every attack except logit lens (at most 47.4%), which they read as signs of deeper unlearning, though still well above chance. Numbers from Łucki et al., Table 1.

blocks.prompt: RMU pushed forget-text activations toward c times a fixed random vector u. At each layer, take the mean difference between the unlearned and original model's activations on forget-topic text, and project that direction out at inference. What happens to WMDP-Bio accuracy?
blocks.reveal: It comes back. Łucki et al. measured 64.7%, slightly above the original 64.4%, with MMLU at 57.3%. Because RMU's loss pushes every forget token toward the same vector, much of its edit is one shared component per layer; a mean difference captures it and projection removes it, while the computation underneath is intact. This is directional ablation, the operation used to erase a refusal direction (optional background: Steering vectors course, lesson 4). Ablating one refusal-style direction at every layer recovered less (54.2%), and NPO and DPO resisted the per-layer version better (45.1% and 50.7%).

blocks.md: Their reading: RMU and NPO behave like safety training. They obfuscate the knowledge rather than remove it, and evaluations that only prompt the model (black-box) cannot tell the difference. As in other security settings, they argue, protections must be tested with adaptive attacks before anyone claims an open-weight model has unlearned something.

**Quantization**, storing each weight with fewer bits by rounding it to one of a small set of levels (16 levels at 4 bits), is an even cheaper attack because users do it routinely to run models on smaller GPUs. Zhang et al. (2024) quantized unlearned models from the MUSE benchmark. For unlearning methods with utility constraints, the full-precision models retained on average 21% of the knowledge meant to be forgotten; after 4-bit quantization they retained 83%. 8-bit models behaved like full precision. Different 4-bit methods gave similar results: plain round-to-nearest; GPTQ, which quantizes weights one column at a time and adjusts the not-yet-quantized weights to cancel the rounding error; and AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization), which scales up the few weight channels that see large activations so they lose less precision. In round-to-nearest with $N$ bits (here $N$ is the bit width, not Lesson 1's dataset size), a signed integer reaches about $2^{N-1}$ on each side of zero, so the step between levels is the largest weight magnitude divided by $2^{N-1}$.

blocks.caption: Round-to-nearest with N bits as written in the paper. Every weight within half a step of a grid point maps to the same integer, so updates smaller than Delta / 2 are invisible.

blocks.title: Why 4-bit rounding erases a small unlearning update

scenes.caption: Six weights of one tensor before and after unlearning. Utility-preserving unlearning uses small learning rates, so each weight moved by at most 0.006. Max |w| = 0.8.

Int-4 round-to-nearest: step = 0.8 / 2^3 = 0.1, so any change smaller than half a step (0.05) can vanish. All six unlearned weights round to the same integer as the originals: the quantized unlearned model IS the quantized original.
Int-8: step = 0.8 / 2^7 = 0.00625, half a step 0.003125. Now 3 of the 6 weights land in a different bin, so part of the unlearning survives quantization.

blocks.md: The paper explains this exactly as the figure does: utility-preserving unlearning uses small learning rates (MUSE and TOFU use peak rates of 1e-5 or below, versus 1e-4 to 3e-4 for pretraining models such as GPT-3 and Llama 3), so most weights move less than half a 4-bit step and $Q(f_{\text{unlearn}}) \approx Q(f_{\text{target}})$: the quantized unlearned model is nearly the quantized original model. The one apparent exception, plain GA, only survived quantization because it had already destroyed the model's utility.

A model that passes forget-set benchmarks in full precision can fail them after an ordinary 4-bit conversion that a user applies for deployment. Any release that relies on unlearning should evaluate the quantized versions people will actually run.

What to do in practice:

- If you need a guarantee (legal deletion), only exact methods give one: retrain without the data, or design training for it (SISA-style sharding, or periodic retraining from filtered data).
- Treat approximate unlearning of open-weight models as output suppression that a motivated attacker can undo. The WMDP authors scope RMU to a closed-model threat model where the provider applies unlearning before serving.
- Evaluate adversarially: paraphrases and other languages, jailbreaks, in-context hints, few-step fine-tuning on related and unrelated data, probes and direction removal on hidden states, and quantization, always against a retrained reference.

Lesson 7 covers methods built to survive these attacks, and lesson 8 runs several of these checks on a real model.

Low scores on forget benchmarks show suppressed outputs, not erased knowledge. Small fine-tunes, probes and even 4-bit quantization can bring "forgotten" knowledge back, because approximate unlearning moves the weights only slightly.

blocks.question: Unlearned model A uses a small learning rate plus a retain loss and keeps 95% of its utility. Model B used plain gradient ascent and collapsed to near-zero utility. After 4-bit quantization, which is more likely to reveal the forgotten knowledge again?
options: A, because its small weight changes mostly fall inside the same quantization bins as the original weights
B, because gradient ascent changes few weights
Neither, quantization only reduces precision and cannot restore information
Both equally, quantization resets every model to the original
blocks.explain: Quantization maps every weight within half a step of a grid point to the same value. Utility-preserving unlearning moves weights by tiny amounts, so the quantized unlearned model is nearly the quantized original, which still knows the facts. Zhang et al. saw 21% retained knowledge rise to 83% at 4 bits; GA was the exception only because it had wrecked the model.

blocks.question: A lab applies RMU to an open-weight model and publishes near-chance WMDP scores as evidence the model is safe to release. What is the strongest objection?
options: WMDP has too few questions to be meaningful
RMU always destroys general capabilities
With open weights anyone can fine-tune on related data, and RMU did not prevent relearning in the WMDP paper's own fine-tuning experiment
Near-chance scores prove the model was never trained on the data
blocks.explain: The WMDP appendix reports that fine-tuning an RMU-unlearned Mistral-7B on the forget corpus recovered performance, and Hu et al. show even benign related data can jog the knowledge back. RMU's stated threat model is a closed model unlearned just before serving, not a public release.

lessons.title: Toward robust unlearning: tamper resistance, distillation, filtering

blocks.md:
Picture two models that both score about chance on WMDP-Bio. One was never trained on the hazardous topics; the other had them unlearned with RMU. Lesson 6 showed what separates them: fine-tuning on ten unrelated examples brings the second model back to about 62%, while the first has nothing to bring back.

So recent work judges unlearning by a stricter test. Lee et al. (2025) state it as **robust unlearning**: the method gets a model, a retain set and a forget set, and its output is scored on two things, the retain performance and the **elicited forget performance**, the best forget score any of several relearning attacks can extract. The reference point is an **oracle** model trained on the same data with the unwanted content perfectly filtered out. This lesson covers three answers, at increasing cost: make the safeguard resist fine-tuning, distill the model into fresh weights, or never train on the content.

Note the shift in definition. Privacy unlearning (TOFU, MUSE) asks for a model that matches retraining without a specific forget set, which really was part of the training data. Capability removal (WMDP) uses forget and retain sets as curated examples of a capability to remove and to keep; they need not be literal subsets of the training data. Similar methods are applied to both, and in both, Lee et al. note, they generally fail to be robust.

Everything here is measured with public proxy benchmarks such as WMDP, whose questions were filtered so that they are not hazardous themselves.

**TAR** (Tampering Attack Resistance, Tamirisa et al., 2024) trains the safeguard *against* simulated attacks, borrowing from meta-learning, the family of methods that train a model to adapt well after a few steps. Here the goal is inverted: the model should end up *far* from what an attacker wants after a few steps.

1. Apply an initial safeguard (for weapons knowledge, Random Mapping, which pushes forget-text hidden states toward fixed random vectors, much like RMU).
2. Each outer step, sample several fine-tuning attacks (64 steps each, varied data and learning rates), run them on a copy, and score the attacked copy with a **tamper-resistance loss**: high entropy, that is near-uniform predictions, on forget-domain text.
3. Update the original weights so the attacked copies do worse, using a first-order approximation instead of differentiating through all 64 attack steps, plus a retain loss (language modelling and staying close to the original's hidden states on retain text).

blocks.title: TAR: train the safeguard against simulated fine-tuning attacks

nodes.label:
Tamper loss:
max entropy on forget

scenes.caption: Start from a model that already has an initial safeguard. It looks safe (27.3% on WMDP-Bio), but fine-tuning attacks bring it back to 61.6% on average.
Inner loop: sample an attack (dataset, learning rate, optimizer) and fine-tune a copy for 64 steps. This is what a real attacker would do.

Score the attacked copy: the defender wants its predictions on forget-domain text to stay near uniform. Maximizing entropy worked better than maximizing cross-entropy, which only spoiled the attacker's first few steps.
Combine with a retain loss on the original weights and update. For Llama-3-8B-Instruct: 750 outer steps on 8 A100 80GB GPUs.

blocks.title: TAR vs RMU on Llama-3-8B, WMDP-Bio (%)

scenes.caption: Before any attack, both safeguards put WMDP-Bio near chance: RMU 31.2%, TAR 28.1%.
Averaged over 26 red-teaming fine-tuning attacks: RMU climbs back to 64.9%, almost the undefended 70.5%. TAR stays at 35.2%.

The price: benign capability (MMLU without the bio subjects) is 65.8% for RMU but 54.7% for TAR. Across the three domains TAR lowers it by 10.6 points on average. Numbers from Tamirisa et al., Table 1.

blocks.md: Read TAR's result with its caveats, which the authors report. It was robust to most but not all test attacks: parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, which trains small added low-rank matrices instead of all weights) and some out-of-distribution learning rates did better. Robustness beyond about 500 steps varied with the data-shuffling seed, and the published numbers cover 500 steps. The authors present TAR as evidence that progress is possible, not as a solved problem. Łucki et al. note it prevents some attacks and not others.

**Distillation** attacks the problem from the other side. Lee et al. (2025) trained a 100M-parameter model on 1B tokens of English (retain) and 1B tokens of Korean (forget), and an oracle on the English alone. They then fine-tuned the full model until its outputs matched the oracle's almost exactly, a KL divergence near 0. Fine-tuned on Korean afterwards, it relearned much faster than the oracle: identical behaviour, but the capability was still in the weights.

A *randomly initialized* student trained to match the same oracle relearned about as slowly as the oracle itself. So they proposed **Unlearn-and-Distill**: unlearn with any method, then distill the unlearned teacher's output distribution into a fresh network using unlabeled pretraining text. The student copies behaviour, and the hidden capability, which the teacher never shows in its outputs, does not transfer.

blocks.caption: UNDO: shrink the unlearned weights by (1 - alpha) and add noise of scale beta, then distill the teacher back into this damaged copy. alpha = 0 keeps the teacher; alpha = 1, beta = 1 is a fresh random initialization.

blocks.md: Distilling into a fresh network costs as much as training one, so **UNDO** (Unlearn, Noise, Distill on Outputs) trades compute for robustness with the perturbation above: more damage, more robustness, more distillation needed. On the synthetic language and arithmetic tasks, its strongest setting matched the robustness of retraining with perfect data filtering while using 60 to 80% of that compute and labelling only 0.01% of the pretraining data (the forget and retain examples). It also improved robustness on WMDP. Distillation of large models into smaller ones is already routine, which makes an unlearning step before it cheap to add.

blocks.prompt: Lee et al. distill an unlearned teacher into a fresh student. The teacher's forget-domain outputs look like a model that never learned the topic, but it still relearns quickly. Predict: will the student relearn quickly too?
blocks.reveal: No, it relearns much more slowly, in some settings about as slowly as the data-filtered oracle. Distillation transfers only what the teacher's outputs show. The latent capability that lets the teacher relearn fast is in its weights and never appears in its outputs, so the student never acquires it. Where the unlearned teacher had a poorer retain-forget tradeoff (RMU on arithmetic), distillation helped less: it is only as good as the teacher's behaviour.

blocks.md:
**Never learning it** is the most direct route. O'Brien et al. (2025), in *Deep Ignorance*, filtered biothreat-proxy text out of the pretraining data of 6.9B-parameter models trained from scratch on 500B tokens plus 50B tokens of annealing (a final phase with instructive and domain-specific data upsampled). The filter has two stages: a keyword blocklist, which about 92% of pretraining documents pass untouched, and a fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier (a small BERT-style text encoder) for the documents it flags. Filtering used under 1% of the training compute. In the released models the pretraining data went through the blocklist alone (8.42% of documents removed); the classifier stage was used on the annealing data.

The filtered models resisted adversarial fine-tuning for up to 10,000 steps and 300M tokens of biothreat-related text, more than ten times what post-training baselines withstood in their tests, with no measured loss on unrelated capabilities. They stayed robust to benign fine-tuning too, which broke the post-training safeguards.

Filtering has limits the authors spell out. A model that never learned a topic can still use it when it is *given* in the prompt, for example by a search tool, so filtering needs a second layer; adding circuit-breaking (a post-training method that reroutes harmful internal representations) helped there. In related work, filtering appeared insufficient to suppress harmful propensities such as toxic text. It is decided before pretraining, so it cannot serve a deletion request that arrives later. And any adversarial evaluation is only a lower bound: a stronger attack may exist.

blocks.title: A ladder of unlearning: robustness against cost

scenes.caption: Fine-tuning methods (lessons 3 and 4) change behaviour on the inputs they saw. They cost minutes to hours, and 10 unrelated examples or removing one direction per layer can undo them.
TAR adds simulated attacks to training. It held through hundreds of fine-tuning steps in its red-teaming, at a cost in benign capability and with known gaps.

Distillation moves the unlearned behaviour into fresh or heavily perturbed weights, leaving latent capability behind. UNDO's strongest setting cost 60 to 80% of a filtered retrain in Lee et al.'s setting.
Filtering pretraining data means the capability is never learned. It is the most robust approach in published tests, but it must be planned before training and does not stop in-context use.

Exact retraining, or SISA from lesson 1, is the only route with a guarantee for deleting a specific training example. Simplified: the costs on this ladder come from different papers, models and attacks, so they are not on one scale.

blocks.md: Robustness numbers from different papers are not comparable. Each uses its own model, data, attack budget and step definition, and Deep Ignorance itself notes that fine-tuning attack configurations are hard to compare. Compare methods only inside one paper's evaluation, and treat any red-teaming result as a lower bound.

Output-level unlearning leaves the capability in the weights. The robust routes either train against attacks (TAR), move the behaviour into weights that never held the capability (distillation, UNDO), or never train on the content (filtering); each costs more compute or more planning.

blocks.question: Lee et al. fine-tune a model until its outputs match a never-trained oracle's almost perfectly (KL near 0), then fine-tune both on forget-domain data. What happens?
options: Both relearn at the same rate, since they behave identically
The oracle-matched model never relearns, because its outputs were fixed
The oracle relearns faster, because it has spare capacity
The oracle-matched model relearns much faster: matching outputs did not remove the latent capability
blocks.explain: Output matching changes behaviour but leaves the weights near a configuration that already encodes the capability, so a few steps restore it. A randomly initialized student matched to the same oracle relearned about as slowly as the oracle, which is the observation behind Unlearn-and-Distill.

blocks.question: Which protection did pretraining data filtering (Deep Ignorance) fail to provide on its own?
options: Resistance to thousands of steps of adversarial fine-tuning
Unchanged performance on unrelated benchmarks
Protection when the filtered information is supplied in the prompt, for example by a search tool
Low accuracy on the biothreat proxy questions before any attack
blocks.explain: Filtered models resisted up to 10,000 fine-tuning steps and kept their general capabilities, but a model can still use knowledge handed to it in context. The authors recommend defense in depth, for example adding circuit-breaking, which helped against such attacks.

lessons.title: Lab: unlearn TOFU authors with NPO, measure it, then quantize it

blocks.md:
Time to run the loop this course has been describing: unlearn, then read forget quality and utility *together*, then check a quantized copy and a relearned copy. There are two tiers.

- **The real setup**, with OpenUnlearning, the framework that replaced the original TOFU code. It packages TOFU, MUSE and WMDP, more than a dozen methods (GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO, RMU among them), and the metrics, including forget quality and six membership inference attacks. It publishes TOFU target and retain models from Llama 3.2 1B up to Llama 3.1 8B. Its scripts assume NVIDIA GPUs, so the commands below were **not run here**; the numbers next to them are the framework's published results.
- **A scaled-down copy run here** on a laptop CPU with 2 threads: same data format, same metrics, same losses, on GPT-2 small (124M parameters).
